name: A Self-Improving Coding Agent
authors: Maxime Robeyns, Martin Szummer, Laurence Aitchison (University of Bristol / iGent AI)
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.15228, Apr 2025; v2 May 2025). Associated with ICLR 2025 Workshop on Scaling Self-Improving Foundation Models (SSI-FM); arXiv comment notes it was submitted as a preprint to NeurIPS 2025.
reflection_type: verbal-self-critique (LLM reflection over an archive of prior agent versions and their benchmark results, used to propose and implement code edits to the agent itself)
feedback_source: environment-reward (a scalar utility computed from benchmark accuracy, wall-clock time and dollar cost over a fixed benchmark set; benchmark scoring uses unit-tests for SWE-Bench/LiveCodeBench and closeness/location checks for the two synthetic benchmarks). Also uses an asynchronous LLM overseer as a self-generated supervisory signal.
iteration_structure: population/evolutionary-style archive loop: maintains an archive of previous agents with their utility scores; each iteration the best-performing prior agent is selected as the meta-agent and instructed to inspect the archive, identify and implement an improvement, then the new agent is re-benchmarked and added to the archive (run for 15 iterations).
reflection_object: agent's own code/architecture: the agent edits its full Python codebase, including tools, sub-agents, prompts, oversight mechanisms, context-management / KV-cache schemes, and editing tools. It eliminates the meta-agent/target-agent distinction (self-referential), modifying output content, action trajectory scaffolding, prompts and reusable tools all at once.
learning_locus: in_context_verbal (no weight update). Despite the source one_line tagging 'gradient_weight_update', the paper explicitly states it is a 'data-efficient, non gradient-based learning mechanism driven by LLM reflection and code updates' — improvement is encoded in the agent's source code, not in model weights.
requires_training: none (no model fine-tuning; learning is realized purely through code/prompt self-edits selected by a utility function)
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge plus verifiable reward: a hand-defined utility function U = 0.5*p_score + 0.25*(cost term) + 0.25*(time term) over benchmark results selects the next meta/base agent; an asynchronous LLM overseer acts as a critic that can intervene or cancel pathological runs. No trained reward model.
distillation_target: model-weights: none. The reflection is distilled into the agent's own source code / architecture (reusable tools, sub-agents, prompts, editing and context-management code) — i.e. into reusable-skill/workflow and prompt artifacts persisted in the codebase and archive, not into weights.
emergent_vs_engineered: scaffold-engineered: improvements are prompt/scaffold/code edits proposed by an LLM reflecting on an explicit archive; the self-improvement loop and utility function are hand-designed. Reflective behavior is not RL-emergent.
memory_type: structured-notes/archive plus skill-library: an archive of all prior agent versions with their benchmark/utility results (queryable via an 'archive analysis' tool); accumulated agent code itself functions as a growing library of reusable tools and sub-agents. Within a run, sub-agents and a scratchpad-style appended context manage short-term state.
memory_persistence: cross-task / cross-iteration: the agent archive and the evolving codebase persist across all meta-improvement iterations and across the different benchmark tasks within a run.
memory_curation_mechanism: population-or-Pareto-selected: all iterations (including failures) are kept append-only in the archive, but the next meta-agent and base agent are selected by argmax of the utility score, so low-utility variants are not propagated as the working agent. Within an agent run, context is curated via sub-agent summarization and periodic diff re-consolidation.
error_localization_granularity: agent-level / block-level (code): reflection identifies which component of the agent system (a tool, sub-agent, prompt, or code module) to add or modify; concrete improvements (e.g. a diff-based 'smart edit' tool, AST symbol locator) are block-level code edits rather than token- or step-level corrections of a single output.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: inter-task: experience (utility over a benchmark suite) is aggregated across tasks and across iterations to drive code changes that transfer to all future tasks, rather than refining a single task's output in place.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: avoidance-only: failed agent variants persist in the archive as examples of what not to do and the next iteration selects a better base agent; there is no mid-trajectory weight-level correction. (Within a run the asynchronous overseer can intervene mid-trajectory to cancel/redirect stuck agents, a form of in-flight recovery at the scaffolding level.)
task_domains: code (software engineering, file editing, codebase navigation), competitive programming, and math/QA reasoning (tool-use and decision-making throughout)
benchmarks: SWE-Bench Verified (random 50-question subset), LiveCodeBench (50 random questions), two synthetic agent-curated benchmarks (a file-editing benchmark and a symbol-location / codebase-navigation benchmark), plus a separate reasoning run on AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond
headline_result: On a random 50-question subset of SWE-Bench Verified, accuracy improved from 17% (initial agent, iteration 0) to 53% (peak, iteration 14) over 15 self-improvement iterations using Claude Sonnet 3.5 (v2) as the main model (with an o3-mini reasoning sub-agent). The full 15-iteration run cost ~$7,000 in API usage.
baselines: Primarily a within-run self-comparison: the initial hand-built agent (iteration 0) versus successive self-improved iterations. Conceptually positioned against ADAS (separate meta-agent/target-agent), Goedel Agent, and the STOP self-taught optimizer (Zelikman et al.) as related prior self-/auto-design systems; for reasoning, against the raw o3-mini-high model.
gains_vs_baseline: SWE-Bench Verified subset: +36 points (17% -> 53% peak; 51% at final iteration 15). Synthetic file-editing benchmark: ~0.82 -> ~0.96 (peak iter 6). Symbol-location benchmark: ~0.35 -> ~0.43. LiveCodeBench: modest, ~0.65 -> ~0.71. Average per-problem time and cost also fell (e.g. mean time ~130s -> ~114s). On reasoning tasks (AIME 2024 + GPQA Diamond) there was little to no improvement: the agent system averaged ~76% while o3-mini-high alone scored 87% (AIME) and 79% (GPQA Diamond), i.e. the scaffolding hurt for strong reasoning models.
compute_cost_profile: Training/search cost: ~$7,000 in API calls for a single 15-iteration self-improvement run; each meta-improvement iteration can take ~1 hour of agent runtime plus a full benchmark sweep. Inference per benchmark problem: roughly $1.6-2.7 cost, ~104-151s wall time, ~0.22-0.30M tokens, ~30-41% cache hit rate (Table 1). Per-problem hard caps: $10 max cost and 300s (5-minute) timeout with a 0.5 timeout penalty.
known_limitations: 1) Hard for the LLM meta-agent to autonomously generate genuinely novel, feasible, high-'taste' improvement ideas each step; bad ideas waste a full edit-plus-benchmark cycle. 2) Strong path dependency / fixation: early feature suggestions (e.g. fixating on caching open files) bias and lower the quality of later suggestions, giving high-variance runs. 3) Short 300s timeouts and per-problem cost caps depress initial scores, so much early 'improvement' is just speed/cost optimization not traditionally captured by SWE-Bench. 4) Agent-system saturation on reasoning tasks: with already-strong reasoning models the scaffolding adds little or can interrupt the model's native chain-of-thought, degrading performance. 5) Risk of running out of signal from a static benchmark set; no weight updates.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: external-tool/verifier plus env-reward: improvement requires running the agent on a benchmark suite with automated scoring (unit tests for SWE-Bench/LiveCodeBench, closeness/location checks for synthetic tasks) aggregated into a utility function. It is not intrinsic-only — selection of which self-edits to keep is driven entirely by external benchmark/environment feedback (no ground-truth labels leaked into the agent's reasoning, but objective verifiable scores are required).
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent: net-positive on longer-horizon agentic/coding tasks (notably SWE-Bench Verified 17%->53%, file editing, navigation, and reduced cost/time), but net-negative-to-flat on reasoning-heavy tasks (AIME/GPQA), where the scaffolding underperformed the bare reasoning model (76% vs 87%/79%). Gains depend on having external benchmark feedback.
calibration_effect: not-measured (the paper does not report calibration/confidence metrics; the closest observation is a 'scaffolding interrupts reasoning models' effect on AIME/GPQA, suggesting added components can degrade strong reasoning-model performance).
failure_attribution_capability: n/a (the system is not a failure-attribution method; however, its asynchronous overseer classifies pathological/off-task behaviors and can attribute and cancel a stuck agent or sub-agent at the agent level, and the archive records which iterations failed).
failure_mode_addressed: Targets agent-scaffolding inefficiencies: slow/token-inefficient file editing, poor code/symbol navigation, and getting stuck in loops or off-task behavior (handled by the asynchronous overseer). Relevant MAST-style modes include error-loops / being stuck, premature termination, and superficial/path-dependent self-reflection (fixation). It also surfaces an overthinking-style failure: scaffolding interrupting a reasoning model's chain-of-thought.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: Code released (SICA reference framework on GitHub). Two agent-curated synthetic benchmarks are defined within the released codebase: a file-editing benchmark (built from SWE-bench repos using consecutive-commit edits) and a symbol-location/codebase-navigation benchmark. No standalone labeled failure-trace dataset is released.
builds_on: ADAS (Automated Design of Agentic Systems; Hu et al. 2024) for the archive + meta-improvement loop; Goedel Agent (self-modifying agent) and STOP / self-taught optimizer for recursively self-improving code generation (Zelikman et al.); self-refinement (Self-Refine, Madaan et al.) and self-reflection (Reflexion, Shinn et al.); prompt-optimization work OPRO and Promptbreeder; open-endedness / autotelic and intrinsically-motivated RL work; AlphaEvolve and AgentSquare as related automated agent-design systems.
extended_by_or_inspired: Cited within the broader 2025 self-improving / self-evolving agent and Darwin-Goedel-Machine line of work (e.g. Darwin Goedel Machine and subsequent self-modifying coding-agent papers) and self-evolving agent surveys; as of mid-2026 it has ~23 citations and is referenced as an early demonstration that a full coding agent can edit its own codebase to self-improve. (Specific named extensions: [uncertain] beyond general citing surveys.)
reasoning_model_native: no / partial: the method itself is scaffold-based and not native to o1/R1-style reasoning models. Empirically the authors find that with strong reasoning models (o3-mini, and they discuss o1/R1) the scaffolding tends to interrupt the native reasoning chain-of-thought and yields little or negative benefit, so it does not hold well for reasoning-model-native settings.
on_policy_distillation_link: No direct link to on-policy distillation: there is no weight update or policy distillation. The authors characterize the code/prompt self-editing as 'in some sense very sample-efficient' and explicitly flag jointly fine-tuning the foundation model with the agent system (citing AlphaEvolve) as future work, which is the closest conceptual bridge to weight-level / distillation approaches.
sample_efficiency: High in the authors' framing: substantial gains (SWE-Bench subset 17%->53%) achieved in only 15 meta-improvement iterations by inspecting the archive of outcomes, described as 'very sample-efficient' since each iteration's detailed archive inspection informs large code modifications. However each iteration is expensive (~1 hour runtime + full benchmark sweep; ~$7,000 total for the run).
